statements.quoted:
A couple thoughts about @RepBaumgartner’s MATCH Act, as we get closer to the @HouseForeignGOP markup on Wednesday. Both revolve around a common theme: the bill is good news for US companies.

1) This legislation will help level the playing field for American companies. Washington has had export controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment (SME) for years now, but our allies lag behind us in some notable ways. It’s bad for US businesses if their international competition can sell to China, but they can’t. The bill would bring allied export controls into alignment with America’s, either by diplomacy or the foreign direct product rule.

2) China’s retaliatory options are limited. This isn’t executive action, but an act of Congress. Think of the big moves Congress has made recently vis-a-vis Beijing: TikTok, outbound investment, BIOSECURE. In all three areas, Beijing didn’t retaliate. What could they even do? They won’t force Congress to reconvene and legislate concessions. That isn’t how this works. Moving competitive actions through Congress is one of the safest ways to help American companies, in part because it complicates Beijing’s response.

statements.quoted:
Great to speak with @PunchbowlNews' @Dareasmunhoz about the MATCH Act—one of several pieces of legislation due for markup by @HouseForeign on Wednesday—which would require companies to apply for a license to provide maintenance service to their lithography machines in China.

I told Punchbowl about our recent research at @AEIfdp diving into the SME supply chain. Julia Torres and I estimate that, absent U.S. action, the hundreds of deep ultraviolet lithography machines imported by Chinese companies will be more than sufficient to manufacture huge numbers of cutting-edge AI chips in the years ahead.

On the other hand:

“If you take away the parts and prevent them from being serviced, then Huawei is going to be sitting on tens of billions of dollars of wasted investment—unable to make chips at a really critical moment in the trajectory of the global AI industry,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at @AEI, said.

Grateful to @RepBaumgartner and @BrianMastFL for their leadership on this important issue.

statements.text: We need to make sure that we get data centers right. They shouldn’t be forced into communities that don’t want them and they should not increase electricity rate rates or water rate rates for homeowners. We also need to make sure that we have a moral, ethical, and legal framework around AI super computing technology that maintains the dignity of human beings and the integrity of the human work ethic. At the same time maintaining a lead on super computing capability versus China is extremely important for our national security and super computers also have tremendous promise for medical science advances that can help Americans live longer and healthier lives. For example, in recent weeks, exciting announcements have been made about discovering types of pancreatic cancer earlier, and reducing rates of sepsis infections both due to AI super computing tech technologies. I look forward to continuing to work in Congress to make sure that data centers and their super computing technology are implemented in a way that is good for communities and good for Americans health wellness and safety.

America must win the AI race, but working families should not be forced to subsidize it. No data center should be forced on a local community. And if a massive new data center needs new power plants, transmission lines, grid upgrades, or water infrastructure, it should pay its own way. This bill protects ratepayers, encourages new generation, and helps communities conserve local water resources.

statements.text:
Very concerned about the economic future of our state. It’s particularly hard for Agriculture right now, and having the highest taxes in the country will really stress the tech ingenuity economy that has funds so much of our growth.  We have some really cool companies expanding in E. Washington, but every single company I talk to mentions concerns about WA’s tax rates, environmental regulations and labor costs. I wish our voters had taken the opportunity to lower their gas taxes and reject an income tax over the last two elections. Obviously they didn’t and I’m sure the voters reasons were multi-faceted, but I hope Olympia’s lawmakers don’t take it as a sign that they can continue on their current path indefinitely. The Federal Government is $40T in debt and the idea that it can run 20% budget defense in perpetuity is going to soon face the cold hard wall of economic reality that is coming. Regardless of the federal $ windfall bailouts provided to the states during COVID and the resounding victory of the D’s in those weeks election, the reality is that the Fed Gov will have to ween states off of the cash rush - particularly given the critical situation of defense upgrades in a rapidly changing world of drone warfare swarms, nuclear proliferation and super intelligence weapons - all things America’s adversaries are pursuing with obsession. That fiscal reality may not come in the next two years, but you can be sure it is coming.

As a certain economist once said, “trends that can’t continue,won’t” and Washington state is on an unsustainable tax, spend and regulate path that is growing in difficulty for the businesses who’s tax revenue pays for our schools, roads and hospitals.

Or, maybe Elon is right and AI will usher in an era that ends all of our fiscal challenges and the growth of government can continue without fiscal concern….(but I wouldn’t count on it). 🇺🇸
statements.quoted:
WA’s tax system now ranks 47th in the country, according to the Tax Foundation’s newly released 2027 State Tax Competitiveness Index. 

Only New Jersey, California and New York rank worse. 

The ranking doesn’t yet include WA’s new 9.9% income tax, scheduled to take effect in 2028. 

I assume that will bring us down to 49th. 

We’ve dropped from #6 to #47 in just 13 years.
